examples_0401

A polynomial, \(p(x)\), is given in factored form. \[p(x)~=~-(x+7)\cdot (x-5)^{2}\]

Which of the following graphs matches \(y=p(x)\)?


First, consider the end behavior. If you expanded the polynomial into standard form, the highest-degree term would be \(-x^{3}\).

\[p(x)~=~-x^{3}+\ldots\]

The highest degree term has a negative coefficient and an odd degree, so the end behavior is "up,down". Or, more formally, \(\lim\limits_{x\to-\infty} p(x) ~=~ \infty\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to\infty} p(x) ~=~ -\infty\).

Next, we consider the roots. From the factored form, \(p(x)~=~-(x+7)\cdot (x-5)^{2}\), it is easy to see (see zero-product property) that \(x=-7\) or \(x=5\) makes the polynomial output 0.

\[p(-7)~=~-(-7+7)\cdot (-7-5)^{2}~=~0\] \[p(5)~=~-(5+7)\cdot (5-5)^{2}~=~0\]

We predict that at \(x=5\) there is a double root (multiplicity of 2) because the corresponding factor is squared. Graphically, we expect the curve to "bounce" off the \(x\) axis at \(x=5\). At the other root, we expect the curve to cut through the \(x\) axis.

Anyway, based on this analysis, we can produce a sign graph of the polynomial.

\(x\) interval or value sign analysis of \(p(x)~=~-(x+7)\cdot (x-5)^{2}\) sign
\((-\infty,-7)\) \(-(\mathrm{neg})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})^{2}\) \(1\)
\(-7\) \(-(\mathrm{zero})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})^{2}\) \(0\)
\((-7,5)\) \(-(\mathrm{pos})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})^{2}\) \(-1\)
\(5\) \(-(\mathrm{pos})\cdot (\mathrm{zero})^{2}\) \(0\)
\((5,\infty)\) \(-(\mathrm{pos})\cdot (\mathrm{pos})^{2}\) \(-1\)


And only one option matches.


A polynomial, \(p(x)\), is given in factored form. \[p(x)~=~x^{2}\cdot (x-3)\cdot (x-7)\]

Which of the following graphs matches \(y=p(x)\)?


First, consider the end behavior. If you expanded the polynomial into standard form, the highest-degree term would be \(x^{4}\).

\[p(x)~=~x^{4}+\ldots\]

The highest degree term has a positive coefficient and an even degree, so the end behavior is "up,up". Or, more formally, \(\lim\limits_{x\to-\infty} p(x) ~=~ \infty\) and \(\lim\limits_{x\to\infty} p(x) ~=~ \infty\).

Next, we consider the roots. From the factored form, \(p(x)~=~x^{2}\cdot (x-3)\cdot (x-7)\), it is easy to see (see zero-product property) that \(x=0\) or \(x=3\) or \(x=7\) makes the polynomial output 0.

\[p(0)~=~0^{2}\cdot (0-3)\cdot (0-7)~=~0\] \[p(3)~=~3^{2}\cdot (3-3)\cdot (3-7)~=~0\] \[p(7)~=~7^{2}\cdot (7-3)\cdot (7-7)~=~0\]

We predict that at \(x=0\) there is a double root (multiplicity of 2) because the corresponding factor is squared. Graphically, we expect the curve to "bounce" off the \(x\) axis at \(x=0\). At the other roots, we expect the curve to cut through the \(x\) axis.

Anyway, based on this analysis, we can produce a sign graph of the polynomial.

\(x\) interval or value sign analysis of \(p(x)~=~x^{2}\cdot (x-3)\cdot (x-7)\) sign
\((-\infty,0)\) \((\mathrm{neg})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\) \(1\)
\(0\) \((\mathrm{zero})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\) \(0\)
\((0,3)\) \((\mathrm{pos})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\) \(1\)
\(3\) \((\mathrm{pos})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{zero})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\) \(0\)
\((3,7)\) \((\mathrm{pos})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{pos})\cdot (\mathrm{neg})\) \(-1\)
\(7\) \((\mathrm{pos})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{pos})\cdot (\mathrm{zero})\) \(0\)
\((7,\infty)\) \((\mathrm{pos})^{2}\cdot (\mathrm{pos})\cdot (\mathrm{pos})\) \(1\)


And only one option matches.

A polynomial is sketched below.


Which polynomial (in standard form) best matches the sketch?

If a polynomial has a factor of \((x-r)\), then there will be an \(x\)-intercept at \((r,0)\).

In this case, the roots (the \(x\)-intercepts) are at:

\[-7,\,-5,\,-3,\,-1\]

Thus, the factors are \(x+7\) and \(x+5\) and \(x+3\) and \(x+1\). So, we know that the function could be written as:

\[y=a(x+7)(x+5)(x+3)(x+1)\]

where \(a\) is some constant.

Lastly, we need to determine whether \(a\) should be positive or negative. In this problem, either \(a=1\) or \(a=-1\). To determine this, look at the right side of the graph. Specifically, we are considering the end behavior of polynomials. Notice that once \(x\) is larger than \(-1\), all the factors will be positive, so only \(a\) will dictate whether the function on the right side is positive or negative.


Notice, on the right side, the function is heading up. I guess more importantly, as \(x\to \infty\) we see the function is positive. This implies that \(a\) is positive. So, in this case, \(a=1\).

\[y=(x+7)(x+5)(x+3)(x+1)\]

Then, we need to EXPAND into standard form. You can do this with repeated box multiplication. You can also use this identity:

\[\begin{align*} (x+a)(x+b)(x+c)(x+d) \equiv & ~ x^4 \\ & + (a+b+c+d)x^3 \\ & + (ab+ac+ad+bc+bd+cd)x^2 \\ & + (abc+abd+acd+bcd)x \\ & + abcd \end{align*}\]

And so, the answer is \(y=x^4+16x^3+86x^2+176x+105\).
